tagline.text: An 1718 Baroque stone church that survived Typhoon Haiyan

location.label: Location
location.text: Guiuan town center, Eastern Samar (Immaculate Conception Parish)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (estimated day trip from Tacloban including transport and meals, per day)

children.text: This is a Jesuit stone church dating to 1718, in the town center of Guiuan at the southeastern tip of Samar. It is known for its seashell ornamentation and carved apostle doors, and after Typhoon Haiyan damaged it in 2013, restoration supervised by the National Museum was completed in 2019. It was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2001.

The church's formal name is the Immaculate Conception Parish Church. It stands in the town of Guiuan in Eastern Samar, at the southeastern tip of Samar Island, and belongs to the Diocese of Borongan. English Wikipedia describes the church as nestled inside a fort. The coordinates are roughly 11.03°N, 125.72°E, and the municipality of Guiuan itself occupies the far southeastern end of Samar.

The Jesuits founded the town of Guiuan in 1595. The first church was made of wood and burned down; the present stone church is said to have been built by the early Jesuits in 1718 and dedicated to the Immaculate Conception. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1768, the parish passed to the Augustinians, and in 1795 it was transferred to the Franciscans. A shortage of priests delayed their arrival, and Fr. Miguel Pérez, the first Franciscan priest of Guiuan, was assigned in 1804.

Even among the Baroque churches of the 18th-century Philippines, the interior of this one is unusual. Seashell ornament is used extensively, and studies have identified at least eight types of shell. The church originally had three carved doors, and two survived until Haiyan. The main door carries the Twelve Apostles, and a side door has carved angels. It is a seaside town's church, with the sea built into its materials and decoration, and that is its character.

The National Museum of the Philippines declared the church a National Cultural Treasure in 2001. On November 8, 2013, Typhoon Haiyan (known locally as Yolanda) made landfall at Guiuan, tearing off the roof and damaging the façade. Fortunately, the stone walls, floors, and crypts survived. Restoration, supervised by the National Museum, was completed in 2019. The story of a church brought back from ruin is the main reason to visit. The same typhoon is recorded as killing 107 people in Guiuan and leaving almost every building badly damaged or roofless, so the church's restoration is also a symbol of the town's recovery. In December 1944, near the end of World War II, the Leyte-Samar Naval Base was built here, and the present airport runway and some concrete foundation slabs remain as traces of it.

The present stone church was built by the early Jesuits in 1718 and dedicated to the Immaculate Conception. The earlier wooden church was lost to fire. Having endured sea winds, earthquakes, and typhoons for more than 300 years, it is worth getting close to see the thickness of the walls and the texture of the stone.

A study found at least eight types of seashell used in the interior ornament. This is a feature unique to a seaside town's church, so we recommend slowly looking up at the ceiling and wall decoration. The current condition of the decoration may have changed after the restoration, so please check on site.

Of the three original carved doors, the main door has carvings of the Twelve Apostles and a side door has carved angels. Two of the doors reportedly survived until just before Haiyan. Rather than only looking at photos, look closely at the grain of the carving.

blocks.title: A church built like a fort

children.text: English Wikipedia says the church sits inside a fort. In 1854 a bell tower was built on top of the fort. Traces of an era of defense against pirates and foreign enemies overlap with a house of worship.

Typhoon Haiyan destroyed the roof and badly damaged the interior. The church was restored with the National Museum of the Philippines and the parish, then handed over and rededicated in December 2019. Look for the restored shell ornaments and the surviving stone walls.

blocks.title: National Cultural Treasure and historical marker

children.text: It was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2001, and on March 18, 2021 the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) unveiled a historical marker. You can read the marker's text for yourself when you visit.

In 1844, under Fr. Manuel Valverde and Fr. Pedro Monasterio, a transept and baptistery were added; in 1854 a bell tower was built on top of the fort; and in 1872 Fr. Arsenio Figueroa built another convent. There is some fun in looking for the traces of a building that grew over many generations.

When you arrive in Guiuan town, go to the Immaculate Conception church first. Walk around the façade and bell tower from outside, and look at the apostle carvings on the main door.

When no Mass is being held, enter quietly and look at the seashell decoration and the sanctuary area. Before taking photos, check any posted rules at the church and take note of the mood among the worshippers.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town. Fish dishes and dried fish (bulad) are common in Guiuan.
If you have time, hire a tricycle to look around the town or nearby villages. Be sure to check the time of the last return vehicle.
The time of the last return trip varies by season and by operator. It is safer to check the time of the last Tacloban-bound trip at the local terminal in the morning before you set out.
Start at the church when you reach Guiuan. Staying in town makes it easy to visit the waterfront. On weekends, ask for the full nightly price and check whether your room has air conditioning.
Walk around the town and the port area near the church. Guiuan Airport inherited the runway used in World War II and has a runway about
long.

By tricycle or a vehicle arranged locally, visit the Sulangan beaches and surf spots on Calicoan Island and return. Surfing is described as best from September to December, but the waves vary with the weather that year.
Calicoan Island is covered separately as another registered destination, so if your schedule allows, plan to combine the two.

items.title: From Manila by air and land

children.text: Guiuan Airport (with a runway about

long) is known to have no regular commercial flights now, after the scheduled passenger service that began in 2012 was discontinued. Check with the airline before departure whether any flights are operating.
From Manila, a flight to Tacloban (TAC) is the most practical option, and from Tacloban you continue to Guiuan overland.
The distance from Tacloban to Guiuan is about
154km
Wikivoyage recommends Silver Star buses, which run from Manila and cross by ferry at Matnog.
Wikipedia says the bus trip from Manila to Guiuan takes about
21 hours
For long-distance buses, check the departure terminal, fare, and whether the service is running with the operator before you leave.
Take a Duptours van from Tacloban New Transport Terminal to Guiuan Integrated Transport Terminal. The September 2026 listing gives
per person one way and about
3 hours 30 minutes
. Ask about the full fare, including any fuel surcharge.
Buses and vans also run from Borongan. The two towns are about
109km
apart.
Check fares and schedules locally.
The church is in the town center, so you can walk from your lodging or go by tricycle.
We cannot guarantee that boats to the island areas run regularly every day. Check at the local port.

Guiuan is open to the Pacific side, where typhoons pass, so the weather varies greatly. The record says that when Haiyan made landfall here on November 8, 2013, it was at about 4:40 a.m. local time. If you plan a trip in typhoon season, travel can be disrupted, so check the weather forecast before you leave.

A church visit is possible all year, but if you want to add a beach or island trip, a period of calm waves and wind is better. If your purpose is surfing, one source says September to December is good.

Wikivoyage lists places such as Tanghay View Lodge and Guiuan Pension House on San Nicolas Street, with fan and air-conditioned rooms from ₱300, and in the Sulangan area Calicoan Villa and Banago Beach Resort. However, many of the listings were last updated in 2016 or 2019, so you will need to check directly whether they still operate and what they charge.

The food is centered on seafood. Wikivoyage lists tamban, suno, sulusugi (swordfish), and bulad (dried fish) as local foods, and mentions GSECC Food Haus on Lugay Street as a restaurant. The town has changed a lot since Haiyan, so treat old restaurant information as a rough guide only.
A day trip from Tacloban is possible, but the journey is long, so check the time of the last return trip first.
The church is a place of worship for its parishioners. Be quiet during Mass and dress modestly.
Look at the seashell decoration and door carvings up close, but do not touch them.
Because the restoration was completed in 2019, ruin photos on old blogs may look different from the church today.
Bring plenty of cash in pesos. The availability of ATMs and currency exchange in Guiuan needs to be checked locally.
Some island areas have weak phone signal and internet, so download your maps in advance.
The historical marker was unveiled by the NHCP on March 18, 2021, so read its text when you visit.
Guiuan lies in the path of typhoons. From June to November, expect possible cancellations and travel disruption, and check the latest weather advisories.
There are no regular flights, so you must travel overland from Tacloban, and it takes a long time.
Bus and van schedules and fares differ between sources, so you need to confirm them locally.
We could not confirm the church's opening hours, admission rules, or photography rules, so follow local guidance.
Interior viewing may be restricted during Masses and events.
Much of the information on island travel and lodging rates is dated, so check again before you book.
An island known for surfing on the Guiuan coast, with beaches and lodging in the Sulangan area. Surfing is described as good from September to December.
The regional gateway city about

from Guiuan, with an airport. Most travelers reach Guiuan overland from here.
An island close to Guiuan town where thousands of Russian refugees from China stayed temporarily from 1949. Check locally whether it can be visited.
